newsReadings.passage:
When the World Meteorological Organization released its State of the Climate Update 2026 on the opening day of the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, it offered a portrait of a planet that has moved decisively beyond the climatic conditions in which modern civilisation developed. The report's central finding is stark: the year 2026 will rank among the four warmest years since systematic records began, extending a sequence in which each of the past twelve years has individually been among the warmest ever measured. The past four years, the WMO notes, are the four warmest on record.

The global average surface temperature for January to September 2026 stood about 1.47 degrees Celsius above the pre-industrial average, a figure the WMO expects to rise further before the year closes. The principal driver is a very strong El Niño event, which has been intensifying since August and is forecast to become the strongest on record by December. El Niño does not itself create new heat; rather, it releases heat stored in the ocean, which is now the warmest ever measured. As WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo observed, the phenomenon gives new meaning to the phrase "off the charts".

The ocean is the great reservoir of the planet's excess heat, absorbing roughly 90 per cent of it, and 2026 is on course to be the tenth successive year of record ocean warmth. Sea level stands at the highest level ever recorded, while sea-surface temperatures set monthly records through the year. On land, the long retreat of the world's glaciers continues: the mass of ice lost in 2025 alone would have filled five Olympic swimming pools every second of the year. Freshwater storage, meanwhile, has been dwindling since 2014.

The consequences are neither abstract nor distant. Hundreds of millions of people in 2026 were exposed to extreme heat that the WMO describes as unbearable, while heatwaves, tropical cyclones and rainstorms are intensifying faster than the historical baselines on which infrastructure and emergency planning were built. In Nepal, a catastrophic collapse of ice and rock, followed by flash floods, illustrated what the report calls compound risk: hazards that arrive together in fragile, warming high-mountain terrain, where a single event can trigger a cascade of others.

What makes the present moment distinctive, the report argues, is the collision of two forces. El Niño acts as a risk multiplier, amplifying weather extremes on a planet already superheated by human-caused climate change. Earth's energy imbalance — the gap between incoming solar radiation and outgoing heat, widened by greenhouse gases — has reached its highest level since monitoring began, meaning the climate system is accumulating heat at an accelerating rate.

Extreme weather in 2026 carried a massive economic and human cost, the report notes, disrupting agriculture, straining health systems and displacing communities. The burden falls most heavily on those least responsible for the emissions that caused it — a reality that underlies the fraught negotiations over adaptation funding at COP31, where the countries most exposed to climate impacts pressed for far greater financial support. For these nations, the WMO's figures are not statistics but a measure of the resources they will need to protect water supplies, rebuild after floods and keep their populations safe from heat that was once considered exceptional.

Yet the report is not merely a catalogue of records broken. Released deliberately on the first day of COP31, it was intended as an authoritative, science-based benchmark against which the conference's negotiations could be judged. Its message, in the words of the WMO, is that the world must do much more to confront the climate crisis — not only by cutting emissions, but by adapting to changes that are already locked in. Whether the diplomats in Antalya heeded that message is a question the final days of the conference would answer.

newsReadings.passage:
For more than a decade, the solid-state battery has occupied a peculiar position in the electric-vehicle industry: universally acknowledged as the technology that could transform transport, yet persistently confined to the laboratory. On 11 November 2026, the American start-up QuantumScape offered the most persuasive evidence yet that this impasse may be breaking, unveiling Osprey, a new all-solid-state battery platform whose early test cells survived 1,000 full charge cycles while retaining about 80 per cent of their capacity.

The significance of the result lies less in the headline number than in the conditions under which it was achieved. The test cell — a two-layer pouch with a 50 by 65 millimetre cathode, roughly 0.3 to 0.4 ampere-hours in capacity — was charged and discharged at a full 1C rate, from zero to 100 per cent state of charge, at 30 degrees Celsius and under just one atmosphere of pressure. Its cathode loading of 5.5 milliampere-hours per square centimetre is in line with commercial electric-vehicle cells. QuantumScape says no other sulfide-based cell has publicly demonstrated such endurance at so low a pressure, and independent coverage has found no published data that contradicts the claim.

Pressure matters because it has long been the Achilles' heel of solid-state designs. Many laboratory cells only perform when squeezed under forces far greater than anything a vehicle pack could sustain, a requirement that adds weight, complexity and cost. Osprey's ability to cycle at ordinary atmospheric pressure removes one of the most stubborn obstacles between the laboratory bench and the production line.

Osprey pairs QuantumScape's proprietary ceramic separator and anode-free lithium-metal design with a solid sulfide cathode, creating a cell that is solid throughout. It builds on the company's existing QSE platform, whose cells — currently being shipped as samples from the Eagle Line pilot production facility in San Jose — still use a liquid catholyte in the cathode. Osprey replaces that liquid with a solid sulfide electrolyte, completing the transition to an all-solid-state design.

The announcement also carried a more eye-catching claim: charging from 10 to 80 per cent in five minutes. Here, the fine print matters. The white paper behind the announcement shows that this feat was achieved at 80 degrees Celsius, or 176 degrees Fahrenheit — well above the temperatures at which electric vehicles normally precondition their packs before fast charging. No room-temperature fast-charge curve was published. The cells were also reported to operate below minus 20 degrees Celsius, and a projected energy density of up to around 1,100 watt-hours per litre remains, for now, a projection rather than a measured result.

QuantumScape is pitching Osprey not as a finished product but as an open platform. Automakers may either use its sulfide cathode, made with a proprietary dry process, or bring their own, with licensing and co-development arrangements on offer. The company says it is already working with automotive partners on early-stage development projects. There is, however, no timeline for Osprey: the white paper describes the process as demonstrated at laboratory scale, with higher-throughput manufacturing still in development and significant work remaining in process engineering.

The verdict, then, is measured. The cycle-life result is the most solid piece of evidence the solid-state field has yet produced under realistic conditions, and it lends credibility to a technology that has often promised more than it delivered. But scale-up, pack safety certification and cost remain unproven, and the headline charging speed depends on conditions no driver will encounter. Osprey may prove to be the moment solid-state batteries left the laboratory — or another reminder that, in battery science, the distance between a promising cell and a car on the road is measured in years, not press releases.
